one_liner: Experimental single-threaded C++ arena allocator with GC smart pointers and heap compaction; beats jemalloc in its own charts, not glibc malloc.
what_it_does: mem++ is a C++20 library that hands out memory from 32 MB mmap'd arenas and offers garbage-collected smart pointers (mpp::MakeShared<T>, MakeSharedN<T>) plus a manual mpp::CollectGarbage() that frees unreachable objects and relocates live ones. A raw mpp::Allocate/Deallocate (malloc/free-like) API also exists but the README marks it deprecated. It is not a malloc replacement: there is no malloc/free interposition, and pointers to GcPtr objects are invalidated by every collection.
how_it_is_fast: Allocation is a bump of the arena's top chunk when it has room; otherwise it does a best-fit lookup in a per-arena treap of freed chunks (ChunkTreap, GetFirstGreaterOrEqualToChunk) and splits the result. Free coalesces with neighbouring chunks and the top chunk, ptmalloc-style, using 16-byte headers and 32-byte minimum chunks. During GC it splits the object graph into connected components, places each component contiguously in one arena, and for singly-linked-list-shaped components lays nodes out in traversal order, which is where the 4-8x iteration speedup over a randomized list comes from.
when_to_use: Research or teaching on compacting GC and locality-improving heap layout in C++.
Single-threaded programs built around pointer-chasing structures (linked lists) whose nodes end up scattered in memory, where a manual compaction pass can pay off.
Experiments comparing bump/treap allocators against jemalloc, which its own complex benchmark shows about 2x slower than mem++ (chart-read values).
when_not_to_use: As a faster general allocator: in its own charts glibc malloc (ptmalloc2, glibc 2.31) and rpmalloc beat it on the 4096-allocation test, and mimalloc and glibc malloc beat it on the 1M-op complex test.
Any multithreaded program: the README says it supports only single-threaded applications, and multithreading is an open low-priority issue (#21).
Production code: the README says it is not recommended for production, the API is unstable (0.3.5), and the last commit was 2023-11-22.
Code that keeps references or raw pointers into GC-managed objects across CollectGarbage(), since compaction invalidates them.
Windows, or projects needing a clear license: Windows support is an open issue (#27) and the repo has no LICENSE file.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond libc/mmap; googletest and google benchmark only for tests and benchmarks
integration.platforms: Unix-like systems with mmap; Windows not supported
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe; single-threaded only per README
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — malloc/free-like mpp::Allocate/Deallocate exist (deprecated) but nothing replaces malloc or operator new globally; the GC API is a different, smart-pointer interface

gotchas: The allocator benchmarks call the deprecated raw mpp::Allocate/Deallocate, not the GC path, so they do not measure MakeShared or CollectGarbage cost.
Allocate and Deallocate scan the arena list linearly (GetSuitableChunk loops over every arena; Deallocate finds the owning arena by range check), so cost grows with the number of 32 MB arenas.
The 'ptmalloc2' column in the benchmarks is the build machine's system malloc (glibc 2.31); the benchmark build uses clang-15 Release with Google Benchmark, 5 repetitions, CPU not stated.
Garbage collection is manual only; automatic collection is an open issue (#45). Compaction moves objects and invalidates raw pointers and references.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick mem++ over SGCL only if you want compaction and locality-driven relocation rather than a concurrent tracing collector; for plain allocation speed, fast-alloc pools or IsoAlloc beat glibc malloc where mem++ does not.
verified_claims_summary: First-party Google Benchmark runs (clang-15, Release, CPU unknown, results only as box-plot images): 4096 random-size allocations take about 590 us for mem++ vs about 1160 us for jemalloc and 960 us for mimalloc, but about 220 us for glibc 2.31 malloc and 150-200 us for rpmalloc; the 1M-op mixed benchmark is about 1010 ms vs jemalloc about 2000 ms and rpmalloc about 1340 ms, but slower than mimalloc (about 670 ms) and glibc malloc (about 700 ms). The 4-8x figure compares iterating a linked list after compaction with the same list randomized in mem++'s own heap.
status_note: Stale since 2023-11-22 with 22 open issues, no LICENSE file and an author warning against production use, so it is reference material only.
